The Work, Torah Thought and Legacy of Rabbi Avraham de Boton (the Author of "Lechem Mishneh")
His Life and Era: The Golden Age in Ottoman Salonika
During the 16th century the city of Salonika, under Ottoman rule, served as the most prominent spiritual, economic and halakhic center of the diaspora of the exiles from Spain [cite: 1]. The arrival of thousands of sages and families from Spanish Jewry and the Portuguese breathed new life into the local community and turned Salonika into a city of yeshivas, Hebrew printing houses and rabbinic courts whose rulings spread their influence across the entire Jewish world [cite: 1]. In an environment rich in Torah scholars and stormy halakhic discussions grew Rabbi Chiya Avraham son of Rabbi Moshe de Boton [cite: 1]. The period was marked by enormous efforts to organize, codify and interpret Jewish law, owing to the communities' severance from their historical centers in the Iberian peninsula and the need to provide a legal and administrative response to the new challenges of life in the Ottoman exile [cite: 1]. The Torah creativity of Rabbi Avraham de Boton grew precisely in this dynamic space, in which the sages were required to create a synthesis between the depth of theoretical Sephardic study and the ability to carry out practical halakhic rulings in communities bustling with commerce and learning [cite: 1, 2, 3].
Rabbi Chiya Avraham de Boton was born in Salonika in the 1540s (around the year 5305 / 1545) to a distinguished family descended from the exiles from Spain [cite: 1, 4]. The name "Chiya" was added to his original name "Avraham" during a severe illness that struck him during his lifetime, as a remedy (segulah) for healing and long life, and so he would sometimes sign his name in his works and rulings [cite: 1]. Despite his lofty standing and his recognition as one of the sages of Salonika, a yeshiva head and a central halakhic authority, his life was relatively short [cite: 1, 2]. He died young, most likely at the age of only 43, while a severe plague was raging in his city [cite: 1, 2]. The year of his death accepted in research and in tradition is 5348 (1588), although in certain sources there are later proposals, for the 1590s [cite: 1, 5]. He was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery of Salonika [cite: 1].
A historical folk legend became attached to his death and burial, attesting to the reverence and admiration that the members of his community felt for him. According to the tradition, Rabbi Avraham died on the eve of Shabbat, and his burial ended very close to sunset, so that the escorts feared that they had fallen into doubt of desecrating Shabbat [cite: 1]. The deep sorrow of the community members subsided when, immediately after the burial, the sun came out from behind the clouds and it became clear that the Shabbat had not yet begun [cite: 1]. Rabbi Avraham de Boton left behind a glorious Torah dynasty [cite: 1]. His sons – Rabbi Meir de Boton (author of "Responsa Maharam de Boton"), Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Aharon – also served in rabbinic and halakhic roles in the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1, 3, 6]. His descendants and sons-in-law, among them the wealthy Yitzchak Algranti, were later involved in publishing and preserving his Torah legacy at the printing house in Izmir and in other communities [cite: 3].
The Salonikan Study Hall: His Teachers and Students
The Torah development of Rabbi Avraham de Boton rests on the foundations of the glorious study hall of Salonika in the 16th century [cite: 1, 2]. His foremost and principal teacher was Rabbi Shmuel de Medina, known by the epithet the Maharashdam – one of the great sages of Salonika, the halakhic authority of the generation and the spiritual leader of the community [cite: 1, 2, 5]. The Maharashdam passed on to his student the analytical approach to study, characterized by rigorous textual precision, by examining the sources of the Talmud and the Rishonim with a critical eye, and by a constant striving for a halakhic decision anchored in economic and social reality [cite: 1, 2, 7]. Rabbi Avraham's attachment to his teacher was very deep, and the thought of the Maharashdam forms a central foundation in the responsa and commentaries of the author of "Lechem Mishneh" [cite: 1, 2, 7].
As a rabbi and yeshiva head in Salonika, Rabbi Avraham de Boton raised many students who continued his path of study and held rabbinic posts throughout the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1]. Among his prominent students mentioned in the literature of the generation are Rabbi Shmuel Chayon, one of the sages of Salonika, who continued his teacher's tradition of study in teaching and ruling, and Rabbi Shabtai Yonah, a respected author and halakhic authority who spread his teacher's Torah throughout the communities [cite: 1]. In the historical literature, such as the book "Kore ha-Dorot" by Rabbi David Conforte, a claim is cited in the name of Rabbi Mordechai Kalai that he wrote parts of the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary in partnership with him [cite: 1]. However, scholars and commentators note that this claim is not supported by other sources and does not reflect the singular creation of the author of the work [cite: 1].
His Central Work: "Lechem Mishneh" on the Rambam's Mishneh Torah
The work that gained Rabbi Avraham de Boton his immortal place in the Torah canon is his book "Lechem Mishneh," a comprehensive and profound commentary on the Rambam's great work, the "Mishneh Torah" [cite: 1, 2, 8]. The process of composing "Lechem Mishneh" includes a bibliographic and dramatic chapter in the history of the literature of the commentators on the Rambam [cite: 1, 9, 10]. Rabbi Avraham began to compose his work as an independent commentary whose aim was to locate the Talmudic sources of the Rambam's rulings, to resolve the objections of the Ra'avad (Rabbi Avraham ben David of Posquières), and to explain difficult perplexities in the Rambam's language [cite: 1, 8, 11].
While he was immersed in writing the work, there came into his hands the commentary of Maran Rabbi Yosef Karo, the "Kesef Mishneh," which was printed at that time [cite: 1, 9, 10]. Once he learned that Rabbi Yosef Karo had already dealt extensively with locating the sources and with answering the Ra'avad's objections, Rabbi Avraham de Boton made a far-reaching editorial decision. He omitted from his manuscript all the explanations and sources that had already been brought in the "Kesef Mishneh," and focused solely on the topics, contradictions and difficulties with which Rabbi Yosef Karo had not dealt or which he had left with "requires further study" [cite: 9, 10, 12]. As a result, his book turned from a merely thorough explanation into a concentrated, profound and sharply argued work, which complements the "Kesef Mishneh" – and from this his name too is derived: "Lechem Mishneh," as an expression of a double portion and an addition to the commentary of Maran [cite: 9, 10, 12].
The interpretive method of the "Lechem Mishneh" rests on several central theoretical principles. First, he focuses on harmonization and the resolution of internal contradictions in the Rambam. Whereas earlier commentators sometimes tended to attribute changes of wording in the Rambam to retractions or to copyists' errors, Rabbi Avraham de Boton assumed as a basic premise that the Rambam was precise in every word [cite: 8, 13]. He developed brilliant distinction-based mechanisms (chilukim) to resolve contradictions between different laws in the "Mishneh Torah," such as resolving the contradiction between the Rambam's attitude to the Greek language in the laws of tefillin and the law he brings in the laws of Megillah [cite: 8, 13].
Second, in places where the "Kesef Mishneh" did not find an explicit source in the Babylonian Talmud, the "Lechem Mishneh" shows broad mastery of the Jerusalem Talmud, the Tosefta, the halakhic midrashim and the structure of the talmudic passages, and extracts the exact source by the power of the depth of his pilpul [cite: 8]. Third, regarding the Ra'avad's objections, Rabbi Avraham does not content himself with rejecting the objection, but penetrates to the depth of the Ra'avad's reasoning and formulates the dispute between him and the Rambam as a whole conceptual-halakhic unit [cite: 11, 14].
Comparison criterion | Maggid Mishneh (Rabbi Vidal of Tolosa) [cite: 1] | Kesef Mishneh (Rabbi Yosef Karo) [cite: 1, 8, 9] | Lechem Mishneh (Rabbi Avraham de Boton) [cite: 1, 8, 9]
Time and place | 14th century, Spain [cite: 1] | 16th century, Land of Israel / Turkey [cite: 1, 8] | 16th century, Salonika [cite: 1, 8]
Central aim | Uncovering the Talmudic source and explaining the plain sense of the Rambam [cite: 8] | An encyclopedia of sources and resolution of the Ra'avad's objections [cite: 1, 8] | Completing the "Kesef Mishneh," resolving contradictions and depth of pilpul [cite: 8, 9, 13]
Study style | Concise, precise and based on the plain sense | Comprehensive, including comparisons to the Beit Yosef and the Tur | Theoretical and distinction-based (chilukim), focused on textual and conceptual difficulties [cite: 1, 8]
Methodological distinctiveness | The first classic work written on the Rambam | Almost complete coverage of all parts of the Yad HaChazakah | Focus on fine points, prevention of conscious duplication and care for linguistic precision [cite: 1, 9]
His Halakhic Work: The Responsa "Lechem Rav" and His Method of Ruling
Alongside his interpretive work on the Rambam, Rabbi Avraham de Boton acted as a central halakhic authority and answered hundreds of halakhic questions sent to him from across the Ottoman Empire [cite: 1, 2, 3]. His answers were collected in his book "Responsa Lechem Rav" [cite: 1, 2, 3]. The book of questions and answers was not printed in the author's lifetime because of his early death [cite: 2, 3]. The work was brought to the printing house in Izmir in the year 5420 (1660) by his grandson, the scholar Rabbi Avraham son of Rabbi Aharon de Boton, in partnership with the wealthy Yitzchak Algranti, who was married to the daughter of the author's son [cite: 3]. The printers and the descendants dedicated five hundred books from the edition as an endowment fund whose fruits would be dedicated to the support of Torah scholars studying in yeshivas, a fact that teaches about the family's communal and scholarly outlook [cite: 3].
The responsa of the author of "Lechem Mishneh" in "Responsa Lechem Rav" reveal a halakhic authority of broad horizons, who combines theoretical depth with descent into the finest details of law and justice [cite: 3, 15, 16]. In his method of ruling, his reliance on the principle of "umdena demuchach" (an evident assessment, the estimation of the intention of the heart) in interpreting deeds and conditions stands out. Rabbi Avraham gave great weight to the presumed intention of the parties in transactions and contracts, beyond the strictly literal formulation of the words [cite: 15]. In a famous ruling he emphasized that when a person deposits or transfers assets to his fellow in order to cover debts, it is not to be assumed that he intended that fellow to sweep up personal profits from the assets, unless this was explicitly stated [cite: 15].
Likewise, in the areas of Choshen Mishpat, he granted decisive halakhic validity to the custom of merchants (the custom of situmta), even in situations where the original Talmudic law poses difficulties, such as an undertaking regarding something that has not yet come into the world, or asmachta [cite: 16]. His rulings also established the absolute legal power of the public and its leaders to undertake obligations and enter into contracts without a predetermined fixed amount, relying on the special status of public matters in Jewish law [cite: 16]. In addition, his discussions of the issues of "beri ve-shema" and the laws of claims and counterclaims show a systematic analysis of the laws of presumptions, with a consistent preference for the monetary presumption (chezkat mamon) where there is no admissible evidence to the contrary [cite: 17].
Scholars of responsa literature and of the Hebrew language, among them Nahum Sokolow, have pointed to the distinctive style of Rabbi Avraham de Boton [cite: 1]. His writing is characterized by clear, orderly, precise and rich Hebrew, which avoids florid awkwardness and presents the legal argument in a logical, transparent and orderly manner [cite: 1]. This lucid style contributed greatly to the acceptance of his rulings among the sages of later generations [cite: 1].
His Influence, Reception and Legacy for the Generations
The Torah legacy of Rabbi Avraham de Boton has been absorbed deeply and fundamentally into the Jewish world of study [cite: 1, 2, 4]. Few are the works that merited entering the status of permanent "armor-bearers" (nosei keilim) printed alongside the foundational text [cite: 1, 2]. Beginning with the printing of the central editions of the "Mishneh Torah" in Venice (such as the edition of 5462 / 1702), the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary was regularly incorporated alongside the "Kesef Mishneh" and the "Maggid Mishneh" [cite: 1, 4, 18]. This incorporation made the "Lechem Mishneh" a required text for every student of the Rambam [cite: 1, 2]. Its ability to resolve severe difficulties and to expose the hidden depth of the Rambam's rulings served as a model for later works, foremost the commentary "Mishneh la-Melekh" by Rabbi Yehuda Rosanes, who continued and broadened the theoretical path paved by the "Lechem Mishneh" [cite: 4, 8].
In the 19th and 20th centuries, with the rise of the yeshiva world in Lithuania and the development of the conceptual-distinction method of study (chilukim), the "Lechem Mishneh" commentary enjoyed a renewed splendor. Yeshiva heads saw in the novellae of Rabbi Avraham de Boton the prototype of the conceptual distinction, since the "Lechem Mishneh" was among the first to show that contradictions in the Rambam do not derive merely from variant readings, but from different legal conceptions of the halakhic concept in different contexts [cite: 8, 13, 14]. At the same time, his answers in the book "Responsa Lechem Rav" became a first-rate source of authority in Sephardic and Ottoman halakhic rulings [cite: 3, 15]. The sages of Izmir, Salonika, Jerusalem and Constantinople cited his rulings on the subjects of communal ordinances, commercial customs, and the laws of ketubot and marriage, and saw him as one of the fathers of the Ottoman legal tradition [cite: 3, 15].
Summary
Rabbi Chiya Avraham de Boton presents an exemplary figure of a Torah scholar and halakhic authority working at the historical meeting point between the Sephardic heritage and the Ottoman center in Salonika [cite: 1, 2]. Although he died with his days cut short, he succeeded in a short time in leaving an indelible mark on the Jewish bookcase [cite: 1, 2]. His editorial decision not to duplicate what was written in the "Kesef Mishneh" of Rabbi Yosef Karo, but to create a concentrated, profound and complementary explanation, produced one of the most brilliant commentaries on the Yad HaChazakah [cite: 1, 9, 10]. In his interpretive work in the "Lechem Mishneh" and in his halakhic responsa in "Responsa Lechem Rav," Rabbi Avraham built a methodological bridge between the plain sense and the Talmudic source and the pilpul and conceptual depth [cite: 3, 8, 13]. His legacy continues to resonate in the study halls and in the halakhic literature to this very day, as an integral part of the study of the Rambam and the teaching of the sages of Salonika [cite: 1, 2, 4].
